title: Knowledge & Logic
overview: Logic is how AI knows things — through precise rules and True/False reasoning rather than guesswork. Learn propositional logic, inference, and first-order logic.

data.body: Propositional logic is based on propositions — statements about the world that can be either true or false. Each proposition is represented using a propositional symbol, usually a letter like P, Q, or R. To reason about more complex ideas, these symbols are connected using logical connectives such as Not, And, Or, Implication, and Biconditional.
A proposition is a statement that is either True or False — never both, never neither. 'It is raining' is a proposition. 'Is it raining?' is not.
Connectives combine propositions into compound ones. AND requires both sides true; OR requires at least one; NOT flips the value. These three operations underlie all of Boolean logic.
P → Q means if P is true, Q must be true. This is how rules are written. The implication only fails when P is true and Q is false.
A set of facts entails a conclusion if the conclusion holds in every world where those facts are true. Entailment is the mathematical definition of logically follows from.

data.text: Logic gives AI the ability to reason with certainty — not probability, not guesswork. Pure deduction.

blocks.title: Evaluating Logic Expressions
blocks.instructions: Run the code to see how AND, OR, and NOT evaluate different logical expressions.
blocks.starterCode:
# Evaluate these logic expressions
print("True and True:", True and True)
print("True and False:", True and False)
print("True or False:", True or False)
print("not True:", not True)
print("(True or False) and not False:", (True or False) and not False)
blocks.solution:
print("True and True:", True and True)
print("True and False:", True and False)
print("True or False:", True or False)
print("not True:", not True)
print("(True or False) and not False:", (True or False) and not False)
blocks.hint: AND needs both True, OR needs at least one True, NOT flips the value.

data.body: A knowledge base is everything an AI agent knows to be true. Inference is how it derives new facts from that knowledge — turning limited information into powerful reasoning.

data.text: How a Knowledge Base is Useful

data.body: A knowledge base stores facts and rules an agent knows to be true. Inference combines them to derive new answers the AI was never directly told.
Once stored, facts are permanent — the AI never forgets. Add one new fact and every related inference updates automatically.
Unlike machine learning probabilities, a KB gives definite answers. If the input facts are correct, every conclusion is guaranteed correct.

data.text: A knowledge base is useful because it turns a handful of facts and rules into an engine that can answer questions it was never explicitly programmed for.
How a Knowledge Base is Useful

data.body: A knowledge base stores everything an AI knows — facts like “It is raining” and rules like “If it rains, the ground gets wet.” Once stored, these facts never fade. The AI combines them using logical inference to derive answers to questions it was never directly asked.

This is what makes a knowledge base useful: it turns a small set of known truths into an engine that can answer an unlimited number of new questions. Add one new fact, and every related inference updates automatically — no reprogramming needed.

blocks.title: Building a Knowledge Base
blocks.instructions: Build a knowledge base with facts and use inference rules to derive new facts.
blocks.starterCode:
# Build a knowledge base with inference
facts = {"has_wings": True, "is_bird": True}
# Rule: if has_wings AND is_bird THEN can_fly
if facts["has_wings"] and facts["is_bird"]:
    facts["can_fly"] = True
    print("Inferred: can_fly")
print(f"Facts: {facts}")
blocks.hint: A Knowledge Base stores facts. Inference applies logical rules to derive new facts.

data.body: Propositional logic reasons about fixed isolated facts. First-order logic lets AI reason about objects, their properties, and the relationships between them — making it vastly more expressive and practical.
FOL introduces named objects: John, London, the number 5. These are constants — specific, individual things in the world the agent reasons about.
A predicate expresses a property or relationship: Human(John), Loves(John, Mary). Applied to objects, predicates produce propositions that are True or False.
∀x means for all x. The statement ∀x: Human(x) → Mortal(x) covers every object in the domain at once — one sentence replaces infinitely many.
∃x means there exists some x. ∃x: Loves(John, x) says John loves at least one thing without naming what it is. Existential quantifiers assert existence without specifics.

data.text: First-order logic extends propositional logic by introducing quantifiers (∀, ∃) and predicates, enabling reasoning about objects and their relationships rather than just simple true/false statements.

blocks.title: Practice Exercise
blocks.instructions: First-Order Logic uses ∀ (for all) and ∃ (there exists) to write rules that apply to entire categories — not just named individuals. Translate two FOL sentences into Python and watch one rule generate conclusions for every object in the world.
blocks.starterCode:
# ∀x: Human(x) → Mortal(x)   means everyone human is mortal
# ∃x: Philosopher(x)          means at least one philosopher exists

humans       = ['Socrates', 'Alice', 'Bob']
philosophers = ['Socrates', 'Alice']
mortals      = []

# Rule 1 — universal quantifier: for ALL humans, conclude mortal
for person in humans:
    mortals.append(person)
    print(f"Human({person}) → Mortal({person}): True")

print()

# Rule 2 — existential quantifier: SOME philosopher exists
exists = len(philosophers) > 0
print(f"∃x: Philosopher(x) → {exists}  (witness: {philosophers[0]})")

print()

# Chained rule: ∀x: Philosopher(x) → Loves(x, wisdom)
for p in philosophers:
    print(f"Loves({p}, wisdom): True")

print()
print(f"One ∀ rule derived {len(mortals)} individual Mortal() facts.")
print("That is why FOL is more powerful than propositional logic.")
blocks.solution:
humans = ['Socrates', 'Alice', 'Bob']
philosophers = ['Socrates', 'Alice']
mortals = [p for p in humans]
for p in mortals:
    print(f"Mortal({p}): True")
print(f"\n∃x: Philosopher(x) → {len(philosophers) > 0}, witness={philosophers[0]}")
for p in philosophers:
    print(f"Loves({p}, wisdom): True")
print(f"\nOne universal rule derived {len(mortals)} mortal facts.")
blocks.hint: ∀x in FOL = 'for' loop in Python. ∃x in FOL = checking if a list is non-empty. That is the direct mapping.

data.body: Knowledge engineering is the process of figuring out how to represent propositions and logic in AI. Practice knowledge engineering using the game Clue as a running example, then extend to two more logic puzzles.
Representing rules and facts from a murder mystery into a logical knowledge base.
Representing a matching puzzle using propositional logic and discovering its limitations.
Using logical inference to determine the exact order and colors of a hidden sequence.

chapters.title: The Clue Example
sentences: A murder was committed by a person, using a tool, in a location. One card of each category (3 people: Mustard, Plum, Scarlet; 3 tools: knife, revolver, wrench; 3 locations: ballroom, kitchen, library) is picked at random and sealed in an envelope.
Players uncover cards and use the Model Checking algorithm to deduce the envelope's contents. In the knowledge base (KB), mark items True if related to the murder, False otherwise.

Formula: (Mustard ∨ Plum ∨ Scarlet)
(knife ∨ revolver ∨ wrench)
(ballroom ∨ kitchen ∨ library)
Starting hand (cards seen by the player: Mustard, kitchen, revolver):
A guess is made: Scarlet, wrench, library — and it's wrong:
Someone shows the Plum card: ¬(Plum). At this point the murderer must be Scarlet (only one left of Mustard/Plum/Scarlet).

One more clue: it's not the ballroom: ¬(ballroom). Now deduce the library (last remaining location). Since the earlier guess (Scarlet, library, wrench) was false and both Scarlet and library are now true, the wrench must be the false part. By elimination, the weapon is the knife.

data.body: Four people — Gilderoy, Pomona, Minerva, Horace — are each assigned to exactly one of four houses — Gryffindor, Hufflepuff, Ravenclaw, Slytherin.

Representing this in propositional logic is cumbersome. Every possible person–house pairing needs its own atomic proposition (MinervaGryffindor, MinervaHufflepuff, MinervaRavenclaw, MinervaSlytherin, PomonaGryffindor, …).
Each person needs an Or over all their possible house assignments:
Formula: (MinervaGryffindor ∨ MinervaHufflepuff ∨ MinervaRavenclaw ∨ MinervaSlytherin)
Mutual exclusivity needs an implication chain so that being assigned one house rules out the others:
Formula: (MinervaGryffindor → ¬MinervaHufflepuff) ∧ (MinervaGryffindor → ¬MinervaRavenclaw) ∧ (MinervaGryffindor → ¬MinervaSlytherin) ∧ (MinervaHufflepuff → ¬MinervaGryffindor) ∧ ...
In simple words: This inefficiency is what First Order Logic solves, but the puzzle is still solvable in propositional logic given enough clues!

chapters.title: The Mastermind Game
sentences: Player One arranges colors in a hidden order. Player Two guesses; after each guess Player One reports only how many colors are in the correct position — not which ones.

chapters.title: Try It Yourself
sentences: Work through a mini deduction puzzle that uses the same kind of logical reasoning as the Clue example and the Mastermind game.

data.text: Knowledge engineering turns complex real-world puzzles into simple logical statements that an AI can solve using model checking.

keyTakeaways.text: A proposition is any statement that is definitively True or False
Connectives AND, OR, NOT, and implication → build compound logic from simple facts
A knowledge base stores all facts and rules the agent believes to be true
Inference automatically derives new conclusions from existing knowledge
Modus Ponens: know P, know P→Q, therefore conclude Q with certainty
First-order logic adds objects, predicates, and quantifiers — vastly more expressive than propositional logic

whatYouLearned: How to represent knowledge as precise True/False statements
How logical connectives and implication combine propositions
How inference engines derive new knowledge from a knowledge base
The power of Modus Ponens and resolution as inference rules
How first-order logic lets AI reason about categories of objects with quantifiers
Why FOL is used in expert systems, legal AI, and theorem provers
